title: Longest a-b-a Subsequence
statement:
You are given a string `s` that contains only the letters `a` and `b`. Call a string **good** if it can be split into three consecutive parts, where the first part contains only `a`, the second part contains only `b` and the third part contains only `a`. Any of the three parts may be empty, so `""`, `"aaa"`, `"bbb"` and `"aabbba"` are good, while `"bab"` is not.

You may delete any characters from `s` (the remaining characters keep their order). Return the length of the longest good string you can obtain.
inputFormat: A single line containing the string `s`.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the length of the longest good string obtainable.
constraints: `s` consists only of the characters `a` and `b`

examples.explanation: Delete the two `b` characters at positions 3 and 4. What remains is `aaaaabbbaa`: five `a`, three `b`, two `a`, which has length 10. Keeping all 12 letters is not good because `a` follows `b` and `b` follows `a`.
Keeping `aba` (positions 1 to 3) is good: one `a`, one `b`, one `a`. The whole string `baba` is not good because it starts with `b`. No good string of length 4 exists, so the answer is 3.
No deletions are needed: the first and third parts are empty and the second part is `bbbb`.

hints: A good string passes through three phases in order: reading `a`s, reading `b`s, reading `a`s. Think of the phase as a state.
Process the string from left to right and keep the best length for each state: `a*`, `a*b*`, `a*b*a*`. What happens to each when you see an `a`? When you see a `b`?
A character can be kept in the current state, or you may already have moved to a later state. State `j` can take the best of states `0..j` before extending.
